Subject: Redwood demo — quick recap + suggested next tests

Alex — thanks again for the demo time earlier today. Quick recap and proposed next steps to help your team evaluate migration risk and parity vs your current hyperscaler setup: 

1) What we saw today
- Latency and throughput on the demo model matched our hosted SLAs for the sequence lengths you provided (50–250 tokens).
- Function-calling and streaming worked end-to-end from your UI (we used the sample invoice flow).

2) Key competitive points you asked about
- API compatibility: Redwood offers an OpenAI-compatible HTTP surface for generation and embeddings; SDKs have a drop-in adapter for most OpenAI client flows.
- Determinism & prompts: We recommend running a prompt-diff test (we can run one using your sample prompts).
- Enterprise controls: VPC/private deployment, KMS, audit logs — all available in Private & Dedicated tiers.

3) Proposed next tests (POC scope) — aim: isolate migration gaps in 2 weeks
- Prompt parity test: run your canonical prompts (sample set attached) against Redwood + current hyperscaler model; compare tokens, responses, and scoring.
- Latency/throughput test: 1k concurrent user pattern with typical batch sizes — capture p95/p99.
- Feature parity smoke: function-calling, streaming, stop sequences, embeddings semantics.
- Cost delta estimate: baseline 1M tokens/month — we’ll provide a modeled comparison.

Next steps
- I’ve attached a one-pager comparing Redwood vs common hyperscalers and a migration checklist. Could you confirm the sample prompt set is representative and share an ideal 2-week window for the POC?

Thanks — I’ll loop in Rishi & Dev for the technical runbook.

—Marissa

Marissa / team / Alex — quick technical note to address the items: 

1) OpenAI-compatible surface
- HTTP endpoints mirror the common OpenAI patterns (POST /v1/chat/completions, /v1/embeddings) and support function schemas. Differences: ours include an explicit model variant header to select quantized vs full float; we return standardized token-level timing metadata in the response.

2) Streaming & function-calling
- Streaming: chunk format uses the same delta/chunks pattern; we include an "is_final" flag in chunk metadata (small extra field but client-friendly).
- Function calling: we support the same JSON schema for declared functions. Caveat: for strict type coercion we recommend running the first 50 calls through our validator (we can do this).

3) SDK migration notes (node/python)
- Node: we provide an adapter that swaps OpenAI client imports to our client with one line change; async iterators for streaming are compatible in >v4.5.0. Edge: some older OpenAI helper libs expect 2xx chunk framing; we provide a polyfill.
- Python: minimal changes required; we surface the same Client.chat.create() flow. Watch for tokenizers — if you use tiktoken, confirm model name mapping (we map common names in the checklist).

4) Hosted test endpoint
- We can provision a short-lived hosted POC endpoint (hosted API mode) with a POC key and traffic shaping limits. If they want VPC isolation, that'll require Dedicated/Private eval (longer lead time).

5) Prompt diffs to watch for
- Tokenization & subtle whitespace handling on long prompts (we suggest running both through our tokenizer and diffing token counts).
- Stop-sequence interpretation when mixed with streaming and function-calls.
- Embedding cosine drift — compare top-k retrieval results with their current index.

I'll attach a migration_compatibility_checklist.xlsx and a short sample_prompt_set.jsonl for them to run. Iʼll also include a suggested test harness (simple node script) to run parity tests.

—Rishi
Rishi Malhotra | Senior Solutions Engineer
